problem: Existing social robot navigation metrics (kinematics, distance, prediction-based) do not capture which agent causally contributed to resolving or escalating a conflict. The prior Responsibility metric only covered de-escalation, started scenarios at full conflict, and was tested on dyadic cases only.
motivation: Humans often compensate for robots' poor navigation, which becomes a nuisance at scale, so evaluating how the conflict share is split between robot and human matters. Metrics that attribute conflict resolution and escalation to specific agents could also serve as evaluation tools and as target functions for planners.
key_idea: Extend the predicted-closest-encounter-based Responsibility metric with a time normalization that models conflict buildup, and add a complementary Engagement metric that measures each agent's contribution to intensifying the conflict.
insight: Responsibility separates agents by foresightedness: in the crowd experiment the median robot R rises from ~0% (ballistic) to ~3% (short-sighted DWA) to ~33% (Social Force), and E rises with it because foresighted agents maneuver more. In the group-splitting experiment, ordinal R ranking matches subjective trajectory quality. The metrics have no normative meaning on their own and depend on context (e.g. R=0 is fine for an agent overtaken from behind). Changing the agent radii moves the metric from collision avoidance to personal-space compliance.
method: Conflict Potential: CP(t)=max(0,1-pDCE/(r1+r2)), where pDCE is the predicted distance of closest encounter under constant-velocity extrapolation from relative position and velocity.
Time normalization: a linear ramp N(t) over a window N_W (12 s) ending at the time of closest encounter (TCE). Conflict C(t)=CP(t)·N(t) models the buildup phase.

Conflict Contribution: CC_agent ≈ C(t) − C_agent,no-change(t), computed by holding one agent's previous velocity. Its positive and negative parts are escalation (CC+) and de-escalation (CC−). The reference behavior is constant velocity.
Time contribution: CC_Time± is the residual change in C not explained by the agents. Time takes the share for conflict that just grows or fades, e.g. collisions or residual conflict at TCE.
Responsibility R_x = ∫CC−_x dt / C_total, and Engagement E_x = ∫CC+_x dt / C_total. C_total is the integral of the summed positive contributions, and shares sum to 1 over {Agent1, Agent2, Time}.

Evaluation protocol: simulated dyadic (oncoming, crossing, overtaking), group-splitting, 20-agent crowd, playing-catch and personal-space scenarios. Agents are ballistic, Social Force, or DWA with 1 m sensor range.

setting.backbone: none (analytical metric); simulated agents use Social Force and DWA controllers
setting.action_space: continuous velocity / heading of simulated agents
setting.privileged: full ground-truth trajectories of all agents; radii and constant-velocity reference behavior assumed

numbers_note: Paper is a metric paper with no navigation benchmark results; only Responsibility/Engagement shares on custom simulated scenarios, so no benchmark numbers are listed.
results: R and E correctly assign responsibility in oncoming, crossing and overtaking dyads (100% to the sole evader, ~50/50 for symmetric Social Force). In group splitting, the ordinal R ranking (left > right > through) matches subjective quality. In the crowd, median robot R is ≈33% for Social Force vs ≈3% for DWA and 0% for ballistic (humans carry ≈99% for ballistic).
limitations: Metrics are dyadic, so second-order effects and social norms are only indirectly captured, and strongly coupled or symmetric agents can produce skewed values.
The constant-velocity reference behavior limits reliability to open-space scenarios; the TCE anchor and window size N_W are design choices that bias against early reactions.
Metrics are not grounded in human trajectory data or user studies, so they lack normative interpretation and are validated only in simulation.
builds_on: Responsibility metric (Wenzel et al. 2025, Spotting the unexpected/responsibility)
